content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has provided comprehensive guidelines for managing individuals with advanced HIV disease. In 2015, WHO recommended that all individuals living with HIV should initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) regardless of their clinical or immune status. Despite this recommendation, a significant proportion of people living with HIV still present for care with advanced disease. Advanced HIV disease in adults, adolescents, and children aged five years or older is defined as having a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or being in WHO clinical stage 3 or 4. All children under five years of age living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease. Advanced HIV disease encompasses individuals newly diagnosed with HIV, those experiencing treatment failure with a subsequent decline in CD4 cell count, and those re-engaging in care after ART interruption. These individuals are at a high risk of mortality, even after starting ART, with the risk increasing as CD4 cell counts decrease, particularly below 100 cells/mm³. Advanced HIV disease is also associated with higher healthcare costs, increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), incomplete immune recovery, elevated viral reservoirs, chronic inflammation, and a higher prevalence of AIDS-related and non-AIDS-related comorbidities. The leading causes of mortality among adults with advanced HIV disease globally include tuberculosis (TB), severe bacterial infections, cryptococcal disease, histoplasmosis, toxoplasmosis, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). TB remains a major cause of HIV-associated hospitalization and death, with significant reductions in TB-related mortality observed over the years due to improved interventions. Severe bacterial infections, including bloodstream, respiratory, central nervous system, and gastrointestinal infections, are also common among individuals with advanced HIV disease, contributing significantly to hospitalizations and mortality. Cryptococcal meningitis is the most common presentation of cryptococcal disease, accounting for approximately 15% of AIDS-related deaths globally, with the majority occurring in sub-Saharan Africa. Other presentations include pulmonary disease, skin, lymph node, and bone involvement. Cryptococcal disease is less common in young children compared to adults. Similarly, histoplasmosis and talaromycosis are important fungal infections associated with advanced HIV disease in specific geographic regions. Talaromycosis, endemic to parts of Southeast Asia, China, and India, is a leading cause of HIV-associated mortality, particularly in individuals with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is a significant cause of mortality among hospitalized adults and children with HIV, although its global burden is poorly characterized due to limited diagnostic facilities. Cerebral toxoplasmosis, caused by the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii, is the most frequent cause of expansive brain lesions in adults with HIV not receiving co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. The prevalence of toxoplasmosis co-infection is particularly high in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean, and North Africa. Malnutrition and wasting syndrome are also critical issues among individuals with advanced HIV disease, particularly in children. Nutritional assessment, counseling, and support should be integral components of HIV care and monitored throughout the care continuum. CD4 cell count remains the best indicator of disease stage and immediate risk of death in individuals with advanced HIV disease. WHO recommends using CD4 testing to identify individuals with advanced disease and guide clinical management. In settings where CD4 testing is unavailable, WHO clinical staging can be used. Point-of-care CD4 technologies and rapid diagnostic tests are valuable tools for identifying individuals with advanced disease and initiating appropriate care. To address the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in advanced HIV disease, WHO recommends a package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support. This package should be offered to all individuals presenting with advanced HIV disease. Randomized controlled trials, such as REMSTART and REALITY, have demonstrated the effectiveness of enhanced care packages in reducing mortality and improving outcomes in individuals with advanced HIV disease. Implementation of these interventions requires careful consideration of diagnostic tools, human resource requirements, quality assurance, and service delivery. ART initiation should not be delayed due to the unavailability of same-day CD4 results, except in cases of suspected TB or cryptococcal meningitis, where ART initiation may need to be deferred to avoid life-threatening complications. In summary, managing advanced HIV disease involves a multifaceted approach that includes early identification, comprehensive care packages, and addressing region-specific comorbidities and coinfections. These efforts aim to reduce morbidity and mortality, improve clinical outcomes, and enhance the quality of life for individuals living with advanced HIV disease.
